47513: The Book and How We Got It
47514: Before we ask how to read the Bible, we ask what it is and where it came from. This unit follows the Bible from events and spoken memories to written scrolls, from scrolls to collections and a recognised canon, from hand-copied manuscripts to the printed and translated Bibles we hold today, in English and in Tamil. Along the way it asks what the Bible is for, why so many voices over so many centuries tell one story, what the manuscript differences really change, and what is gained and lost when God's word crosses from Hebrew and Greek into our own languages.
47516: Why do we have a Bible at all, what is it for, and how can so many writers over so many centuries tell one story?
47517: The Bible is God's gift of a shared memory: a library written by about 40 people over roughly 1,500 years, not written to us but given to us, so that we might know the God who has finally shown his face in Jesus. Scripture bears witness to the Word; it is not a rule book for its own sake.
47518: A library, not a single book
47519:
The word 'Bible' comes from the Greek *ta biblia*, which means 'the books'. That plural is a good place to start. The Bible is a library: 66 books in most Protestant Bibles, more in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles (Lesson 2 explains why). It holds stories, laws, songs, proverbs, prophetic poems, letters, biographies of Jesus and visions.

The two halves are called 'Testaments'. A testament here means a covenant: a binding, relational agreement. The Old Testament tells of God's covenant with Israel. The New Testament tells of the new covenant made through Jesus, which the prophets had promised (Jer 31:31-34; Luke 22:20). So from the start the Bible is not a list of rules floating in the air. It is the record of a relationship.

Jesus himself named the Scriptures of his day by their three parts: 'the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms' (Luke 24:44). Jewish readers still call this collection the *Tanakh*, from the first letters of Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).
47521:
God speaks because he wants to be known. People forget, so God's acts were written down as a memorial. After the battle with Amalek, Moses is told to 'write this in a book as a memorial' (Exod 17:14). The book of the law was placed beside the ark as a witness (Deut 31:24-26). Habakkuk is told to write the vision plainly on tablets so that a runner may read it (Hab 2:2).

The New Testament gives its own reasons. John says his Gospel was written 'so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name' (John 20:31). John's first letter says the apostles write what they have seen and touched so that readers may share their fellowship 'with the Father and with his Son' (1 John 1:1-4). Paul says the older Scriptures were written 'for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope' (Rom 15:4).

So the purpose is relational: life, fellowship, hope, and being made 'wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus' and equipped for good work (2 Tim 3:15-17). Jesus warned against missing that purpose. Some people searched the Scriptures carefully but would not come to him, the one the Scriptures pointed to (John 5:39-40).
47522: Not written to us, but given to us
47523:
Every book of the Bible had a first audience. Paul's letter to the Corinthians is addressed 'to the church of God that is in Corinth' (1 Cor 1:2), and the letter to the Galatians 'to the churches of Galatia' (Gal 1:2). When Paul asks Timothy to bring the cloak he left at Troas (2 Tim 4:13), he is not asking you to bring a cloak. Old Testament scholar John Walton often puts it this way: the Bible was written *for* us, but it was not written *to* us.

This is not a way of making the Bible less important. It is a way of honouring how God actually gave it. We are like people reading someone else's letters, which God has deliberately handed to us. Paul says the stories of Israel 'were written down for our instruction' (1 Cor 10:11). They were first lived and written by others; then they were given to us.

The practical result is simple. Before asking 'What does this mean for me?', ask 'What did this mean for them?' Then ask how God's purpose for them, now fulfilled and clarified in Jesus, speaks to us. Lesson 12 on culture, date and audience develops this in detail.
47525:
The Bible was written by about 40 authors over roughly 1,500 years. (The learner's notes say 1,000 years; on the traditional dating the span is longer, from Moses around 1400 BC to the book of Revelation around AD 95.) Many critical scholars date much of the Old Testament later, so on their view most of the writing falls within about 1,000 years. Either way it is a very long time. The writers include a shepherd-king, priests, prophets, fishermen, a tax collector, a doctor and a tentmaker. They wrote in three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek) and in places from Babylon to Rome.

Yet these voices tell one story. God creates a good world (Gen 1:31). Humans turn away and the world is broken (Gen 3). God promises to bless all nations through Abraham (Gen 12:1-3), forms Israel and frees them from slavery (Exod 19:4-6), promises a king from David's line (2 Sam 7:12-16), disciplines and restores them, and then comes himself in Jesus. Jesus taught his disciples to read the whole story this way: 'beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself' (Luke 24:27). The story ends with a renewed creation where God lives with his people (Rev 21:1-5).

Many believers rightly see this unity as a sign of God's hand. It is also honest to say that unity is not sameness. The Bible holds real conversations within itself: Job and Ecclesiastes push back on easy readings of Proverbs, and Chronicles retells Kings with different emphases. The single story is carried by many voices, not one flat voice.
47526: God did not bypass the human authors
47527:
The Bible does not describe itself as words dropped from heaven. Luke tells us he researched carefully, used eyewitness reports and wrote an orderly account (Luke 1:1-4). Paul's personality is everywhere: his anger (Gal 5:12), his tears (2 Cor 2:4), even a moment where he cannot quite remember whom he baptised (1 Cor 1:14-16). Jeremiah dictated his words to a human secretary, Baruch (Jer 36:4). Each writer has his own vocabulary and style.

At the same time, the writers spoke from God as they were 'carried along by the Holy Spirit' (2 Pet 1:21). The picture is of a ship carried by the wind: the ship really sails, and the wind really moves it. Inspiration is not dictation. God breathed life through real people, in their own languages, cultures and personalities, and did not switch them off. Unit 2 explores what 'God-breathed' means.

Christians have often compared this to the incarnation. In Jesus, God became fully human without ceasing to be God. In Scripture, God's word comes in fully human words. This is why Hebrews says God spoke 'at many times and in many ways' through the prophets, but has now spoken in his Son, who is the exact imprint of God's nature (Heb 1:1-3). The written words are a true and inspired witness; Jesus is the Word they witness to (John 1:1-18; John 5:39-40).

47557: How do God and the human writers work together?
47558: Christians agree that God and humans were both involved in writing the Bible. They differ on how. Each position below is held by thoughtful people. Unit 2 looks at these more closely.
47559: God alone (the writer is a pen)
47562: Some popular piety; rejected by almost all theologians, including the strictest
47563: God dictated each word and the writer simply recorded it. Few theologians hold this, because the books plainly show different styles, research and emotions.
47565: B. B. Warfield, J. I. Packer, the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978)
47566: God guided the writers so that every word is what he intended, while using their own personalities and styles. This view explicitly denies dictation.
47568: Herman Bavinck and the Dutch Reformed tradition
47569: The Spirit worked through the whole life, culture and character of each writer, like sap through a living tree.
47572: God is the author of Scripture, and the human writers are also true authors who used their own powers. Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted recorded for our salvation.
47574: As Jesus is fully God and fully human, Scripture is fully God's word in fully human, culturally shaped words. Its human marks are not embarrassments but part of how God chose to speak.
47575: Witness to the Word, read through Jesus
47576: Karl Barth; in a Jesus-centred form Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd
47577: Scripture is the inspired witness to God's self-revelation, which is fully given in Jesus. It honestly records God's people's developing perception of him, and Jesus is the lens for reading it.
47579: Many secular and liberal critical scholars
47580: The Bible is the literature of ancient Israel and the early church, valuable for history and faith, but not inspired in any special sense.

47582: How you think of the Bible shapes what you look for in it. Compare three common approaches.

47591: Confusing: is it allowed or not?
47592: Look for a verse that settles it.
47593: Reported, not endorsed; the story shows its pain (Gen 29:30-31) and Jesus returns to God's design (Matt 19:4-8).
47595: Takes the Bible's truth claims seriously.
47596: Fits the Bible's own shape and Jesus' reading of it (Luke 24:27).
47597: Turns a relationship into a contract; misses genres.
47598: Pulls verses out of their setting.
47599: Can become vague if it ignores clear commands; needs care in defining what is 'Christlike'.
47600: Scripture bears witness to the Word; it is not the Word himself (John 5:39–40). Jesus is the measure that measures all.
47602: Passage supplied in the learner's course notes
47604: A phrase he has popularised in sermons and books
47605: The New is in the Old concealed; the Old is in the New revealed.
47606: Popular English rendering of *Questions on the Heptateuch* 2.73 (Latin: Novum in Vetere latet, et in Novo Vetus patet)
47607: Evangelical: God's written word, fully trustworthy
47608: J. I. Packer, John Stott, D. A. Carson; the Chicago Statement (1978)
47609: The Bible is God's inspired, written word. Because God cannot lie, what Scripture teaches is true and carries God's own authority. It is the final standard for faith and life, and Christians read every part as God's word to his people.
47610: It follows Jesus' own high view of Scripture (Matt 5:18; John 10:35) and gives the church a stable standard that stands above any leader or culture. It takes every book seriously.
47611: Critics say it can treat the Bible as a flat rule book, ignoring genre and the human, historical side. Defenders reply that careful evangelical scholars insist on genre, context and Christ-centred reading.
47612: Catholic: Scripture within the living Tradition
47614: Scripture and Sacred Tradition flow from 'the same divine wellspring' and together form one sacred deposit of the word of God. The Church's teaching office (Magisterium) serves the word and interprets it. Scripture has God as its author and the human writers as true authors.
47615: It matches the historical fact that the Bible came to us through the worshipping church, and it guards against every reader becoming his own pope.
47616: Protestants worry that Tradition and church authority can end up standing over Scripture rather than under it. Catholics reply that the Magisterium is 'not above the word of God, but serves it' (*Dei Verbum* 10).
47617: Orthodox: Scripture as the heart of Holy Tradition
47618: Georges Florovsky; Kallistos Ware, *The Orthodox Church*
47619: The Bible is the supreme expression of God's revelation, but it lives inside the church's worship, prayer and the writings of the Fathers. It is read, sung and prayed in the liturgy more than studied alone.
47620: It keeps Scripture tied to worship and the community, and it draws deeply on early Christian reading.
47621: Others ask how Tradition can correct itself if Scripture is always read through it. Orthodox reply that the Spirit guides the whole church, not single readers or single councils.
47622: Jesus-centred: Scripture as witness to the living Word
47623: Karl Barth (older form); Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Peter Enns, Bill Johnson ('Jesus is perfect theology')
47624: The written words are inspired and true witnesses, but the Word of God in the fullest sense is Jesus (John 1:1-18). God spoke partially through the prophets and fully in the Son, the exact imprint of his nature (Heb 1:1-3). So the whole Bible is read with Jesus as its key and goal (John 5:39-40; Luke 24:27).
47625: It follows how the New Testament itself presents Jesus as the climax of revelation, and it keeps Bible study from becoming detached from knowing God. It guards against using verses to justify violence.
47626: Critics warn of a slide toward Marcion (who rejected the Old Testament), note that Jesus himself fully affirmed the Old Testament (Matt 5:17-18) and spoke of judgement, and ask who decides what is 'Christlike'. Defenders reply that they keep the whole Old Testament as inspired and read the Jesus of all four Gospels, including his warnings.
47627: Jewish: the Tanakh as Israel's covenant library
47628: Jon Levenson; Adele Berlin and Marc Brettler (eds), *The Jewish Study Bible*
47629: The Hebrew Bible is the treasured record of God's covenant with Israel, read together with the Oral Torah and centuries of rabbinic discussion. Its centre is Torah and the ongoing life of the covenant people, not a coming Messiah who has already arrived.
47630: It reminds Christians that these Scriptures belonged to Israel first and that their first meaning matters. Jesus and the apostles were Jewish readers.
47631: Christians read the same texts as finding their fulfilment in Jesus (Luke 24:44). Jewish readers answer that the Christian reading often overlooks the plain meaning for its first audience.
47632: The Bible as an owner's manual
47633: The Bible is God's instruction manual for life ('Basic Instructions Before Leaving Earth'). Every page tells us what to do, and if something is in the Bible, God approves of it.
47634: Most of the Bible is story, poetry and letters, set inside a covenant relationship. Even the Ten Commandments begin with a rescue: 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt' (Exod 20:2). Much of the narrative reports what happened without approving it: Jacob's two wives bring rivalry and pain (Gen 29:30-31), and kings are told not to multiply wives (Deut 17:17). Scholars such as Gordon Fee, Douglas Stuart and Christopher Wright stress reading each genre as the kind of writing it is.
47635: Traditional scholars agree the Bible is not a manual, but they add that it truly does command, and that love for Jesus is shown in keeping his commands (John 14:15). Narrative also teaches, so the answer is not to treat stories as optional but to ask what they teach in context.
47636: A manual reading can make violence or polygamy look approved because they appear in the text. A covenant-story reading asks what God was doing with these people and where the story is heading.
47637: Every promise is addressed to me personally
47638: Jeremiah 29:11 ('I know the plans I have for you') is God's personal promise that my career, health or relationships will go well.
47639: Jeremiah wrote this to Jewish exiles in Babylon, telling them to settle down because the return would come only after seventy years (Jer 29:10). The 'you' is plural: the whole people. Many who first heard it would die in exile before the promise was fulfilled. Scholars such as John Walton and Christopher Wright point out that the promise is about God's faithfulness to his people over generations.
47640: Careful traditional scholars note that the God who kept that promise is unchanging, and Paul says all God's promises find their 'yes' in Christ (2 Cor 1:20). So believers may draw real hope from the verse, as long as they hear it first as a word to a community in exile.
47641: Reading it as a personal guarantee can crush people when life goes badly. Reading it in context gives a deeper hope: God stays faithful to his people even through long, painful seasons.

47655: How did events, memories and writings become one Bible, and who decided which books belong in it?
47656: The Bible grew in stages: God acted, people remembered and retold, writers wrote, communities copied and collected, and over centuries the church recognised the books it had already been living by. The councils did not create the canon; they recognised it.
47657: First the events, then the memories
47658:
Before there was a Bible there were events: a family called out of Mesopotamia, slaves freed from Egypt, a man from Nazareth crucified and raised. The first response was not writing but remembering out loud. After the Red Sea crossing, Moses and Miriam sang (Exod 15:1-21). Parents were told to explain the story when their children asked what the commandments meant (Deut 6:20-25).

This is called *oral tradition*: teaching passed on by speaking, singing and repeating, usually in a community that cares about getting it right. Ancient people trained their memories in ways most of us never do. Paul quotes an early summary of the gospel that he 'received' and 'delivered', two words used for handing on a tradition carefully (1 Cor 15:3-8). Luke says the accounts of Jesus were 'delivered to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word' (Luke 1:1-2).

Oral tradition is not a game of whispers. Scholars such as Richard Bauckham argue that eyewitnesses stayed active in the early churches and acted as a check on the stories. Others think more change happened in the retelling. How much the tradition was controlled is debated, but nearly all agree that the gospel was preached for some decades before the Gospels were written.
47660:
The Bible itself shows writing happening. Moses 'wrote down all the words of the LORD' (Exod 24:4). Joshua wrote in 'the Book of the Law of God' (Josh 24:26). Isaiah's teaching was sealed among his disciples (Isa 8:16), and Jeremiah dictated his messages to Baruch, rewriting the scroll after the king burned it (Jer 36:1-32). King Hezekiah's officials copied out proverbs of Solomon (Prov 25:1).

The writers also used earlier sources, and sometimes name them: the Book of Jashar (Josh 10:13), the Book of the Wars of the LORD (Num 21:14) and royal chronicles (1 Kgs 14:19). These books are lost, but the Bible's authors drew on them. In the New Testament, Paul's letters were written from about AD 50 and passed between churches (Col 4:16). The Gospels followed, most scholars think between about AD 65 and 95.

How long the writing and editing took is debated. Traditional Jewish and Christian belief holds that Moses wrote the Torah in substance. Many critical scholars think the Torah and the historical books were shaped by several sources and editors over centuries, reaching their final form during or after the exile. Many evangelical scholars accept some later editing (Deut 34 records Moses' death) while holding that the core goes back to Moses. Either way, God was at work in the whole process, not only at a single moment of writing.
47662:
Writings became a collection as God's people used them. When a 'Book of the Law' was found in the temple in King Josiah's day, it led to national repentance (2 Kgs 22:8-13). After the exile, Ezra read the Law aloud to the whole people while Levites explained its sense (Neh 8:1-8). By Jesus' time the Scriptures were known in three parts, the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms or Writings (Luke 24:44). Around AD 95 the Jewish historian Josephus described a fixed set of 22 books (counting several together), which most scholars match to the 39 books of the Protestant Old Testament.

The word *canon* comes from the Greek *kanōn*, a measuring rod. It came to mean the list of books the community measures its faith by. Jews call their canon the Tanakh and count 24 books; Protestants divide the same content into 39.

There is a real difference between churches here. Greek-speaking Jews used the Septuagint, a translation that also included books such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach and 1 and 2 Maccabees. The early church mostly read the Septuagint, so these books were widely read. Catholics call them *deuterocanonical* ('second canon') and confirmed them at the Council of Trent in 1546. The Orthodox churches include them and a few more. Protestants, following the Hebrew canon, call them the Apocrypha: Luther printed them between the Testaments as 'useful and good to read' but not equal to Scripture.
